The story makes sophisticated use of metaphor throughout the narrative to deepen its emotional and thematic resonance. Most notably, the writer uses an extended metaphor comparing the ruined, burned-out armchair to the woman, Claire, and her marriage. Like the chair, the couple maintains the external structure of a relationship ("still occupied the space of a chair; you could still name its parts"), while the core where intimacy and comfort should exist has been gutted ("Only the place where a human body was meant to rest had been hollowed out to the springs"). This is directly linked to Claire when her face is described as having "the flat, calcined blankness of things that have already been through the fire." 

Additionally, the writer employs smaller, striking metaphors—such as the couple arguing with "exhausted choreography," the city contracting into "private, hurrying capsules," and municipal flood warnings acting as a "liturgy of encroaching ruin"—to establish a vivid, melancholic atmosphere.
